*Coming Out of the Ice* is a 1982 memoir by Soviet dissident and former political prisoner **Yuli Daniel**, though it was actually written and published **under the pseudonym "Yuli Daniel"**—wait, correction: that’s inaccurate. Let me clarify carefully, because there’s a common point of confusion here.

🔍 **Important Clarification**:  
*Coming Out of the Ice* **is not by Yuli Daniel**—it is by **Yevgenia Ginzburg**, a Soviet writer, teacher, and Gulag survivor. Her full name was **Yevgenia Solomonovna Ginzburg** (1904–1977). The book is her acclaimed two-volume autobiographical account—*Journey into the Whirlwind* (1967) and *Within the Whirlwind* (1979)—but *Coming Out of the Ice* is **not the original Russian or standard English title** of either volume.

✅ So—here’s the accurate, verified information:

### 📘 *Coming Out of the Ice*: The Facts  
- **Author**: **Yevgenia Ginzburg** (1904–1977), Soviet educator, journalist, and Communist Party member who was arrested in 1937 during the Great Purge.  
- **Original Russian Title**: *Крутой маршрут* (transliterated: *Krutoy Marshrut*), meaning **“A Hard Road”** or sometimes translated as *“The Steep Route”*.  
- **English Publication**:  
  - First English edition (abridged) was published in **1967** under the title **Journey into the Whirlwind**, translated by Paul Stevenson and Max Hayward.  
  - The **complete, unexpurgated two-volume English edition** (including material suppressed in the earlier version) was published in **1981** by Harcourt Brace Jovanovich under the title:  
    ➤ ***Within the Whirlwind*** (Vol. 1: *Journey into the Whirlwind*; Vol. 2: *Within the Whirlwind*).  
- **“Coming Out of the Ice” is NOT an official title** used in major English editions—but it *has appeared* as:  
  • A **misremembered or conflated title**, possibly mixing up Ginzburg’s work with other Gulag memoirs (e.g., Alexander Solzhenitsyn’s *The Gulag Archipelago*, which references “coming out of the ice” metaphorically), or  
  • An **alternate/variant title used in some non-English editions** (e.g., certain Dutch or German translations use ice/winter metaphors), or  
  • A **confusion with the 1982 U.S. television film adaptation**, which was indeed titled ***Coming Out of the Ice*** (see below).  

### 📺 The 1982 TV Film  
- **Title**: *Coming Out of the Ice*  
- **Year**: 1982  
- **Network**: NBC (U.S.)  
- **Based on**: Yevgenia Ginzburg’s memoir *Krutoy Marshrut*, adapted for television.  
- **Starring**: **Mary Tyler Moore** as Yevgenia Ginzburg — a controversial casting choice due to Moore’s lack of Slavic background and the film’s Hollywood-style dramatization.  
- **Reception**:  
  - Criticized by scholars and Gulag survivors for historical simplification, emotional melodrama, and deviations from Ginzburg’s nuanced, restrained prose.  
  - Praised at the time for bringing Soviet repression to mainstream American audiences.  
  - Notable for being one of the first major Western dramatizations of Stalinist terror based on a survivor’s firsthand account.  

### 📚 About the Memoir Itself (*Krutoy Marshrut*)  
- **Scope**: Covers Ginzburg’s arrest in 1937 (as a “Trotskyite” despite being a lifelong loyal Bolshevik), 18 years of imprisonment and forced labor—including time in the Kolyma gold-mining camps (among the harshest in the Gulag), and her eventual release and partial rehabilitation in 1955.  
- **Style**: Combines meticulous detail, psychological insight, dark irony, and moral clarity. Ginzburg avoids polemics but exposes systemic cruelty through quiet observation and human dignity.  
- **Significance**:  
  - A cornerstone of Gulag literature—ranked alongside Solzhenitsyn, Shalamov, and Dostoevsky’s *House of the Dead*.  
  - Unique in its perspective: written by a highly educated, ideologically committed woman who gradually awakens to the regime’s betrayal—making her disillusionment especially powerful.  
  - Smuggled out of the USSR in the 1960s; first published abroad in Italian (1967), then in English and other languages.  
  - Ginzburg wrote it secretly between 1963–1967, relying on memory and notes preserved on scraps of paper—she had no access to documents or diaries.

### 📜 Why “Ice”? The Metaphor  
While not the official title, “coming out of the ice” is a resonant metaphor used throughout the memoir:  
- Kolyma was known as *“the land of the white death”*, where temperatures plunged below –60°C.  
- Ginzburg describes the *“ice”* as both literal (frostbite, frozen tundra, frozen rivers) and figurative (the chilling dehumanization of the terror, emotional numbness, frozen hope, the “ice age” of Stalinism).  
- Her “coming out” signifies survival, moral reawakening, testimony, and re-entry into humanity after years of systemic erasure.

### 🔚 Legacy  
- *Krutoy Marshrut* remains essential reading for understanding Stalinism, totalitarianism, and the resilience of the human spirit.  
- Ginzburg died in 1977, before seeing her full memoir published in Russian (first complete Russian edition appeared in 1988, during *glasnost*).  
- Today, authoritative English editions are titled:  
  ➤ ***Journey into the Whirlwind*** (Vol. 1)  
  ➤ ***Within the Whirlwind*** (Vol. 2)  
  (Published together as *Journey into the Whirlwind & Within the Whirlwind* in modern omnibus editions.)

---

✅ **In summary**:  
There is **no book officially titled *Coming Out of the Ice* by Yevgenia Ginzburg**, but the phrase refers to:  
1. The **1982 NBC television film** *Coming Out of the Ice*, starring Mary Tyler Moore, adapted from Ginzburg’s memoir *Krutoy Marshrut*; and  
2. A **descriptive or metaphorical reference** to Ginzburg’s harrowing survival and testimony—her emergence from the physical and moral “ice” of the Gulag.  

The authentic, indispensable work is **Yevgenia Ginzburg’s *Krutoy Marshrut*** — best read in English as ***Journey into the Whirlwind*** and ***Within the Whirlwind***.
